1	# Writing a test
2	
3	**gated test**
4	: Test that the gate's suites run.
5	
6	**green**
7	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as passed.
8	
9	**red**
10	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as failed.
11	
12	**`XXX` test**
13	: Gated expected failure. It asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed.
14	
15	## A test program
16	
17	A test program has this form:
18	
19	    component Name
20	    export Executable
21	
22	    (* declarations *)
23	
24	    run(): () = do
25	        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
26	    end
27	
28	    end
29	
30	- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
31	- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
32	- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`, for values of any type. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
33	- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
34	- Under walk, a numeral does not bind to `NN32` or `NN64`, and a numeral with a radix point does not bind to `RR32` (ledger row 454). Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`.
35	
36	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
37	
38	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
39	
40	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
41	- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
42	- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
43	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
44	- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test with such a `.test` file is green if the program loads and runs clean.
45	
46	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:
47	
48	- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
49	- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
50	- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
51	- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series, by the comment in `OtherCompilerJUTest.java`. Put no new test there.
52	
53	The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
54	
55	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
56	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
57	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
58	    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
59	                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
60	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
61	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
62	
63	A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. For example:
64	
65	    tests=EqualityRung1
66	    link
67	    run
68	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS
69	
70	## How `XXX` works
71	
72	- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
73	- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
74	- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
75	- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
76	- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
77	- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.
78	
79	## How a defect is recorded
80	
81	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:
82	
83	1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
84	2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
85	3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.
86	
87	If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. A probe that only measures and reports is an example. The change that next works there writes the test.
88	
89	## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass
90	
91	1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
92	2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says.
93	3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.
94	
95	The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix, such as one that guards a behaviour that works today, has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.
96	
97	In your report, quote two to five lines of the failing run, if there is one, and the passing line, each with its command. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A probe that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key. The harness checks both, so they are part of the suite's verdict.
98	
99	An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.
100	
101	## Writing an `XXX` test
102	
103	In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.
104	
105	- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test, with `compile` and `compile_err_contains=<the refusal's message>`.
106	- For a code-generator wall (`compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
107	- For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over the component:
108	  - `NameLink.test`, a plain name, with `tests=XXXName` and `link`. It is red if the link reports static errors, but green on an exception.
109	  - `XXXName.test`, with `tests=XXXName` and `run`, and no `link`. Its run uses the plain file's link, so run the two files in one call of `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`, the plain one first.
110	  - The program prints `REACHED` in `run()` before the part that fails. The `XXX` file checks it with `run_out_contains=REACHED`, or with `run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED` if the run dies before `run()` prints. Never use `run_out_contains=PASS`.
111	  - Example: `compiler_tests/XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW.test` and `BoxDotSpellingsRungWLink.test`.
112	
113	Show the first `XXX` test that your change adds, and only the first, working through the harness (`harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`), from its place in a gated test folder. A direct compile and run does not show this. Run it twice:
114	
115	1. As it is: the harness must report an expected failure.
116	2. Changed for one run so that the defect does not show, then restored: the harness must report it red. For example, add the missing declaration to the test program, set the expected string to what the run prints, or, in a run-time pair, remove the part that fails.
117	
118	## Promoting an `XXX` test
119	
120	If your change fixes a defect that has a gated `XXX` test, the fix turns that test red. To find such a test, search the gap ledger (`records.md`): a row's reproducer names it. Also list the `XXX` files: `git ls-files 'ProjectFortress/*XXX*'`. Then promote it:
121	
122	1. Before you edit the code, remove the prefix: give the test a plain name by its topic. Rename each file with `git mv` (`committing.md` gives the commit), or with `mv` if the file is not committed yet. Rename each `XXX` name inside: the `component` line, and in a compiled test the `tests=` lines and keys. Change a run-time pair as below.
123	2. See the plain-named test fail through the harness on the base's code, as "The order", step 2, says.
124	3. Make the fix and see the test pass.
125	
126	A run-time pair keeps its three files, renamed without `XXX`. For example, `compiler_tests/NatRtTask` was promoted so in `fd5cb4864`:
127	
128	- `Name.fss`, with `component Name`. The program asserts its values, then prints `PASS` last.
129	- `NameLink.test`: `tests=Name` and `link`.
130	- `Name.test`, in place of `XXXName.test`: `tests=Name`, `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`.
131	
132	## Names, comments, citations
133	
134	- Name a test by its topic. Give it one comment line that says what it checks, with no pointer to a record.
135	- In a test, cite the specification by file and section or entry, never by line: `opr-overview.tex, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators"`. In the library chapters, name the entry too: `basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE`.
136	- If your change breaks a line of a test that the team wrote, respell the line and keep the value that it checks. Keep every assertion. List each line's before and after in your report.
137	- If your change touches mutable state, a field, an `atomic` block or library code that writes shared state, run its checks at one thread and at four. The same holds for the Java of tasks, transactions or the class loader. `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` and the suites force four threads. For one thread, run the program directly with the prefix `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (a compiled program: `compiler.md`, "Running"), and check its exit code and output.

- F-245 **Checking symbolic operators for overloading added 186 errors to the distance in the compiled checker, measured at `d97001d19`, whose code is climb batch 20's gate, with crashes caught per name; climb batch 21's first run clears them: 54 by known library fixes (F-276), 124 by the index bound (F-278) and 8 by the exclusion test (F-277).** As the stage ran there, the 186 were 185 errors and three crashes on `||`, in `List`'s api and component and `String`'s component, "E is not in the kind env": a checker crash that no fix or design clears (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md` section 1.3). The check was turned on in a copy of the checker whose three loops admit every operator; the checker as built skips them (row 584). On climb batch 21's base the stage gives 191, the distance's 5 and 186 more, the three crash lines printed beside them (`compile-ladder/plan-21/probes/full-check-base.tsv`); each rung alone, 137 with the known fixes, 67 with the index bound and 183 with the exclusion test; the planner measured the run's library text together at 5, nothing come (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-21.md`, section 4). The two designs, a bound on the subscripts' index type (124 errors) and a vector plus a number beside a vector plus a vector (8), are P-156's and P-157's. The probe's candidates S1, an index bound with a rule for tuple indices, and A2, `Vector` and `Matrix` leaving `AdditiveGroup`, clear them with nothing new; A3, the scalar `+` and `-` dropped, also clears the 8; S1 is built, and the exclusion test in A2's place. The largest families were the subscripts over a generic `Indexed` (124) and `String`'s four concatenation operators, `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///` (40). An earlier measurement, at `d212b2c1f`, counted 205; batches since cleared `FlatString`'s pair (2; F-259) and 20 of the 21 `^` errors (F-263), and added 3: `|_|` 1 and the scalar `+` and `-` 2. Walk's meet check, which also skips symbolic operators and judges neither `String`'s pairs, the subscripts, `^` nor `=`, refused only `EmptyString`'s `||` when widened the same way in the first probe of these operators. Detail: `perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md` sections 0 to 2; `perf-probes/symbolic-operators/REPORT.md` section 1.5.

- F-81 **In the interpreter's library, every Meet Rule pair inside one type that the compiled checker checks has a declaration on its meet. The checker skips operators whose names are symbols (row 584); checked, their pairs give the errors of F-245.** `String`'s juxtaposition is three top-level operators, since two functional methods with `self` at different positions have no meet. `String`'s `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///`, which paired `(a:Any, self)` with `(self, b:Any)`, the shape the specification refuses, are now three top-level operators each too (F-276). F-245's measurement found other invalid pairs, among them `Indexed`'s three subscripts in 17 types, valid since the index bound (F-278). The rung that added these meets also set the declared types listed in report section 1 to what their bodies answer. Elsewhere in the library some still differ, such as `__bigOperator2`'s fused branch (F-85). Gated by `tests/LibraryMeetDeclarations.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-meets/REPORT.md` section 1.

- F-249 **Under walk, a program that imports only the prelude reaches the string objects' own `||` through the top-level `opr ||(a:String, b:String)`, whose `typecase` calls them.** The string objects' own `||` are those that the objects `FlatString` and `EmptyString` declare, and that the trait `Concatenable` declares for the objects `CatString` and `SubString`. `FortressLibrary`, where the top-level `||` is declared, sees them only where an api that it imports states them: `FlatString`'s api does, and String's api states `Concatenable`'s and `EmptyString`'s three each (`Library/String.fsi:17-19`, `:29-31`). So `"s" || "t"` is a `FlatString` of depth 0, as it was while `String`'s abstract `opr ||(self, b:String)` stood (F-276); a top-level meet with `Concatenable`'s body, which a probe tried, gave a `CatString` of depth 1. Gated by `tests/StringConcatenationFamiliesWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-symbolic-library/REPORT.md` section 12, decision 3; `perf-probes/symbolic-operators/REPORT.md` sections 2.2 and 2.4.

- F-259 **An object or trait whose `extends` clause names `Any` alone is an `Object` on both paths, but the library's `Index` (F-278), and such an object expression under walk, and `String`'s two top-level `||` over `Any` convert by the library's own way.** The pre-disambiguation desugaring that both paths run gives such a clause `{Object}`, as it gives an empty one, and leaves `Any`'s, `Object`'s and the library's `Index`'s own declarations as written; a clause that names only `Index` (and `Any`) gets `Object` beside it. `opr ||(a:Any, b:String)` is `("" || a) || b` and `opr ||(a:String, b:Any)` is `a || cast[\Object\](b).asString` (top-level since F-276); `FlatString`'s api states its component's header, with no `opr ||(a:FlatString, self)`. So a tuple or `()` concatenates on the left of a string, and a function or a tuple of seven or more elements beside one raises `CastError`. The team test `extendAny` prints `Infinity`, and the distance's three `String` sites are gone: 34 to 31, the count 30 to 28. Tests: `tests/ExtendsAnyIsObjectWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/ExtendsAnyIsObject.test`, `tests/ConcatAnyOnLeftWalk.fss`; the distance stage. 1	(* A tuple type whose element types are all Index types is an Index and no Object, so a static parameter bounded by Index takes ZZ32 and its pairs and triples, and the subscript beside the range subscript runs at each. *)
     2	component TupleIndexBoundWalk
     3	export Executable
     4	
     5	ident[\I extends Index\](x: I): I = x
     6	
     7	trait Cells[\I extends Index\]
     8	    opr[i: I]: String
     9	    opr[r: Range[\I\]]: String
    10	end
    11	
    12	object Grid[\I extends Index\]() extends Cells[\I\]
    13	    opr[i: I]: String = "one index"
    14	    opr[r: Range[\I\]]: String = "a range"
    15	end
    16	
    17	object Slot(n: ZZ32) extends Index end
    18	
    19	kind(x: Object): String = "object"
    20	kind(x: Any): String = "any"
    21	
    22	oneIndex(x: Index): String = "an index"
    23	
    24	run(): () = do
    25	    assert(ident(3), 3, "ident takes a ZZ32 at its bound Index")
    26	    assert(ident((1, 2)), (1, 2), "ident takes a pair of ZZ32 at its bound Index")
    27	    assert(ident((1, 2, 3)), (1, 2, 3), "ident takes a triple of ZZ32 at its bound Index")
    28	
    29	    g1 = Grid[\ZZ32\]()
    30	    assert(g1[4], "one index", "the subscript at ZZ32")
    31	    assert(g1[0#2], "a range", "the range subscript at ZZ32")
    32	    g2 = Grid[\(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]()
    33	    assert(g2[1, 2], "one index", "the subscript at a pair")
    34	    g3 = Grid[\(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]()
    35	    assert(g3[1, 2, 3], "one index", "the subscript at a triple")
    36	
    37	    m: Matrix[\RR64,2,2\] = matrix[\RR64,2,2\](2.0)

    39	    assert((m + 1.0)[0,1], -2.0, "a matrix plus a number")
    40	    assert((1.0 + m)[0,0], 3.0, "a number plus a matrix")
    41	    assert((m MAX 0.0)[0,1], 0.0, "a matrix MAX a number")
    42	    assert((0.0 MAX m)[0,0], 2.0, "a number MAX a matrix")
    43	
    44	    a = array[\ZZ32\](2,3).fill(0)
    45	    a[1,2] := 12
    46	    assert(a[1,2], 12, "a rank-2 array read and written at a[i, j]")
    47	    assert(a[(1,2)], 12, "a rank-2 array read at a pair")
    48

    50	    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]((1, 2)), true, "a pair of ZZ32 is an Index")

    52	    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]((1, "a")), false, "a pair with a String element is no Index")
    53	    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]("a"), false, "a String is no Index")
    54	    assert(instanceOf[\Index\](()), false, "() is no tuple type and no Index")
    55	    assert(instanceOf[\Index\]((1, ())), false, "a pair with a () element is no Index")
    56	    assert(instanceOf[\Object\](3), true, "a ZZ32 is an Object")
    57	    assert(instanceOf[\Object\]((1, 2)), false, "a pair of ZZ32 is no Object")
    58	    assert(kind(3), "object", "a ZZ32 goes to the declaration over Object")
    59	    assert(kind((1, 2)), "any", "a pair of ZZ32 goes to the declaration over Any")
    60	    i: ZZ32 = 1

content.content:
- P-155 **The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over.** Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as `MAX`, so `+`, `^`, `||`, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that stay additive groups by a change to the checker's exclusion test. Row 584: the check and its rungs.

- P-156 **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.** Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`; `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes it. So a subscript that takes one index and a subscript that takes a range never apply to the same value, and the pair is a valid overloading at every instance. A tuple type whose elements are all `Index` types is itself an `Index`, on both paths and in the specification: a typing rule that changes no value, so `m[i, j]` passes its tuple `(i, j)` as before. Why: it is the team's own fix for this pair (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`), its "magic" read as subtyping. A `where` constraint `I excludes Range[\I\]` was weighed and not taken: the team left such a constraint as an open question, and the code generator refuses a `where` clause in a declaration's header. `Index` stands beside `Any` and `Object`, outside `Object`: it is declared `trait Index extends Any`, which the desugaring and walk keep as written and the traits chapter names as an exception to the rule that every trait extends `Object`, so a tuple of indices is an `Index` and never an `Object`, and P-42's tuples stay out of `Object`, as the specification's `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` keeps them. `BoundedRange`, which cannot take the bound, since the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56), keeps its narrowed `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` under the method condition `where { I extends Index }`, the library's form for a member that applies at some instances only; after the switch-over the code generator's refusal of a method with a `where` clause stops it too, as it stops `SumReduction`'s two `distribute`s (row 701). Row 783: the subscript pair.

- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` stay additive groups, and the overloading check's exclusion test reads the self type and the static parameters' bounds, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** The team's `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and the library's generic block of `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar (P-88) stays beside them. With symbolic operators checked (P-155), the checker refused 8 such pairs, though no call fits both: a vector's own `+` takes two vectors, the block's `+` an array and a number, and arrays exclude numbers. So the exclusion test reads a self-typed trait's `self` as `C[\X\] & X`, the fact that P-146's extender rule guarantees, and its existential reduction reads the static parameters' bounds (P-152); specificity and the Return Type Rule keep the plain signatures. Why: it keeps both the team's library as written and the revival's block, and it was his first stance; taking vectors out of `AdditiveGroup` would have bent the team's design for a gap of the checker. Reading bounds is the POPL 2019 paper's own reduction. Probe A1 measured it (`perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`): the 8 gone, nothing else moved.

- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS-history.md:1234:- P-135 **The coordinator rewrite's goals.** The `coordinator` skill is rewritten by a heavier process than `fortress-repo`'s, since the coordinator acts in several roles that work well and must not be lost to an ill-considered change. Its goals: one home for how the coordinator works, the protocol retired and its rules that bind workers moved to `fortress-repo`; every kind of record with one home and a stated purpose, the informal homes (the handover's first section, the held list, PLAN's old rule sections, the boot note's standing lines) retired or folded in, and the skill saying plainly what goes where; a lighter boot that keeps his awareness (the coordinator knows the project without him, never re-asks a decision, never sends a worker to measure again what is on record), the open question being FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX (their form, a grouping by topic, what they repeat of each other, what is always loaded and what is looked up), settled on evidence and a trial boot, not assumed; FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving workers' briefs; no role lost (executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst); the `fortress-repo` writing standard. The skill is tiered: a core always loaded, and sections loaded when the coordinator switches into a mode of work that is not needed all the time (running and reviewing a batch, process engineering, a post-mortem, among others), as the workers' skill separates building from exploring; the coordinator's modes are identified and described first. The batch workflow is in scope, since it is improved whenever it shows a problem. `cloud-container` follows by the `fortress-repo` method. The rewrite rests on the frontier model's own habits, not on a system designed around them: "I don't want a system of hundreds little rules with potentially contradicting dos and don'ts." The skill guides lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to him in each situation, and the record is organized as the model organizes knowledge by itself: "Organization of the knowledge base should reflect the model's second nature, never fight it", which he names the rewrite's highest risk. So the natural baseline of the current models, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, is established before the design, and the design starts from what this project's environment adds to it: his review on a phone, dictation by speech to text, holding the open items of a long dictated message (preventing the wall-of-text spiral and recovering from it), and keeping a large body of project knowledge in order. The map also gives where each record home came from and which model made it. The map of the shape the rewrite starts from is `coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md`. The skill is written from scratch by an Opus writer, from the sort of the rules against the baseline (what is kept, and the facts stated instead of rules), the map's problems to design against, and the writing principles; the writer does not read the existing skill, which is not refactored. A check against the sort's list after the draft shows whether anything kept was lost, and then the cold read follows as usual. A rule is kept when the failure it guards against is on record; the interview's self-report decides no drop, since the two disagree exactly on the rules that matter (the clock, closed decisions), and the interview showed only the record's default shape, a short current-state file with decisions and history apart, which is kept without instruction. The two sorts carry the map's handles, not the rule texts, and are not what he or the writer judges a rule by.

# The C series and the APL side quest: state and what comes next

## Where the work stands

Retired on 2026-10-12: the current state of the work is the first section of `coordinator/PLAN.md`, and what is in flight is `coordinator/BOOT.md`; the text this section held is in `microgpt-run-c-handover-history.md`, "The first section as retired on 2026-10-12".

## Read first

`explorations/coordinator/README.md`, `FACTS.md` and `POSITIONS.md` first (created 2026-09-15): the established facts and Pavol's positions, so that nothing there is re-derived or re-explained. Then the rest of this section.

*Superseded in part, 2026-09-26:* the work branch is `main`, pushed and then fast-forwarded to `claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` (protocol § 4); the sealed-tree rule ended with the unsealing of 2026-09-17 (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md`); stop-hook reminders are declined silently (protocol § 4). The rest of this paragraph is from the C series' era. `explorations/protocol.md` is the operating manual and stays in force: Opus workers for probes, exploration, replication, runs and compilation; design, implementation and articles in this thread; worker code reviewed against the design before it is committed; Pavol decides. Work branch `claude/handover-reading-vn8zgr`; commit and push as you go; fast-forward `main` after every push with `git push origin claude/handover-reading-vn8zgr:main`; if `main` diverged because Pavol committed there, merge `origin/main` into the work branch, never rewrite history. The only other branches this thread pushes to are `claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` (the Fable session's branch, when Pavol asks) and, when asked, `transcripts`, `blinded-fable`, `transcripts-blinded`. Commit footer exactly the two lines in protocol.md; no model identifier in any committed file except the process records' "models" row. Never modify the historical language, compiler, runtime or shipped library ("we are not unsealing anything"). Never commit copyrighted decks or Karpathy's `microgpt.py`. Plain register: short sentences, no flourish, no caveats that are not real problems, no headers under 500 words. AskUserQuestion is broken here; artifact watch subscriptions are refused. A worker cancelled by Pavol is not resumed or relaunched unless he asks. Commit in-progress snapshots when the stop hook nags, with "worker running" in the message. Pavol's standing objection, answered once: the programs contain no explicit threading; every `for` is Fortress's implicitly parallel loop on the runtime's work-stealing pool

- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, save in the overloading check's exclusion test (F-277), and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). When it landed, the distance stage's self-type class fell from 29 errors to 0 (the distance from 85 to 55), one measurement on that tree. Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled default body that returns `self` dies at class load with a `VerifyError` when the trait's self-type parameter is an object type, as in `object Pt(…) extends Shape[\Pt\]`: an open defect (row 695). The rule refuses, rightly, two team declarations, each an open row: the demo `trips.fss`'s `generator` (row 710) and `PureList`'s `List` (row 355). Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7.

- F-227 **The compiled checker replaces a closed trait among an intersection's conjuncts by those of its listed types that no other conjunct excludes, only where that excluding conjunct names no type variable or inference variable, so `K ∩ R[\T\]` stays as written; below a union, an inference variable takes the whole union as one upper bound, and a type variable is tried through its bound as well as against each member.** The code is `normConjunct` and, for the union cases, `pSubInner`, in `scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`. So a call through a parameter bounded by a closed trait and a bound that excludes one of its listed types checks, and a generic declaration so bounded, beside a declaration on the closed trait, is a valid overloading (rows 686, 687, 689, 690 and 711). A call whose argument's type only carries the parameter, `Box[\T\]`, under a ground second bound, stays refused: an open defect (row 712). Before the checker kept such an intersection as written, it accepted, through the expansion, an overloading on a question that Appendix I lists as not settled; it refused the pair while it kept the intersection, and accepts it again since its exclusion test reads the static parameters' bounds (F-277; `compiler_tests/OverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion`); walk refuses it at load (row 713, contested; `tests/OverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusionWalk`). #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'

We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime
type and of every supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of
\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Object}.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
Every tuple type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.
No other type encompasses all tuple types.
Tuple types cannot be extended by trait types.
A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type
other than \TYP{Any}.
---
In addition, every trait except \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object}
implicitly extends the trait \TYP{Object}
if it does not do so explicitly.
This relation must form an acyclic hierarchy
rooted at trait \TYP{Object}.
---
The above overloaded declarations are not really a valid overloading.
We want to say that the type variable \VAR{I} extends a type, say,
\TYP{Index} which either excludes \EXP{\TYP{Range}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}
or is a supertype of \EXP{\TYP{Range}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}.
However, we cannot say that because when we invoke that subscripting method,
we write \EXP{a[1, 2, 3]} where the arguments are passed as a tuple,
\EXP{(1, 2, 3)}.  If we want to use \TYP{Index},
we need a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to something of type \TYP{Index}.

implements the methods of this trait.  The immediate subtypes of the trait
